notes:
**Windows** — run `ruze_0.0.33_x64-setup.exe`.
**Linux** — `flatpak install ruze-0.0.33.flatpak`, then `flatpak run com.ruze.chat`.
**Android** — sideload `ruze-0.0.33.apk`. arm64 devices, Android 8.0 or newer.

---

### Added

- **You can take back something you said to a friend.** Deleting a message
  worked in a channel and not in a conversation, which read as an oversight and
  was one. It is offered on your own messages now, in both places, and in a
  conversation it goes from their copy as well as yours — and from your phone as
  well as the machine you sent it from.

  A conversation is two documents, each written from one end, and you hold the
  pen for exactly one of them: everything you have ever said. That is why it is
  only offered on your own — not a rule the app enforces, but the shape of the
  thing. A word of theirs cannot be reached from here at all.

  What gets written is a standing note that the message is gone, not only the
  removal of it. The removal by itself would be undone by the first peer that
  synced from an older copy; the note travels with the conversation, and every
  read on either side applies it, so a message that comes back from somewhere
  stays off the screen.

- **Link previews load themselves, and a setting stops them.** A YouTube, X,
  Instagram, image or video link used to sit there as a card saying "Play video"
  until somebody clicked it — which is a fair description of the link it was
  already showing. The preview now loads as you reach the message, so the video
  is there, ready.

  Ready, not playing. Nothing starts on its own: a player that loaded because it
  was on screen waits for you, and only one you asked for by clicking starts. A
  channel that begins four videos at you as you scroll into it is worse than a
  click.

  It costs something, and Settings › Content filtering says so and turns it off.
  A preview comes from whoever hosts it, so with this on, scrolling to a message
  tells YouTube or X or Instagram that you read it. Off, every link goes back to
  a card naming the host it would load from, and fetches nothing at all until
  you click it.

### Changed

- **A friend who is not online cannot be called.** The three call buttons are
  greyed when nobody of theirs is reachable, and say so when you point at
  them. Ringing somebody who is not there opened a room, switched on a camera
  and played a ringback to a line nobody was listening on.

- **The header over a conversation has a line under it, and the faces have
  lost their caption.** The chip in the corner said "here now" beside the
  faces of whoever is; the faces were already saying it. And the header now
  sits above a rule rather than floating over the column, so it reads as a bar
  the conversation scrolls beneath.


- **The two tabs at the head of the room list are icons.** Servers and Friends
  were words, in a column narrow enough that they were the widest thing in a
  bar whose whole job is to be got past. They are a grid and a pair of people
  now — a fixed pair that never changes and never grows, which is the case an
  icon is actually good for. Each keeps a name for a screen reader, says what
  it is on hover and on keyboard focus, and carries its unread count on the
  corner of the glyph rather than beside a word that is no longer there.

- **One column instead of three.** The strip of server icons and the channel
  list beside it have become a single column of cards. The server you are in is
  a card with its channels on show; the others are a line each, and the people
  you know are a section underneath them rather than a separate screen behind a
  button.

  The old arrangement spent 60 pixels on a rail and 220 on a list before a word
  of conversation, and the first of those two existed only to choose which of
  the second to show. There is one column now, and it is wider — which it can
  afford to be, because it replaced two.

- **A room shows who is in it before you go in.** A voice channel used to be a
  row in a list with a number beside it. It is a block on the server's card
  now: the people in it, who is speaking, and — when you are in it yourself —
  your own microphone, where you can see whether it is open. An empty room stays
  a quiet line; one with people in it is the loudest thing on the card, which is
  the right way round for an app whose point is that somebody else is there.

- **Who is here is a chip you open, not a column that is always there.** The
  member list was a third panel taking two hundred pixels of a window whose
  middle is the point of it, and it collapsed to a sheet anyway whenever the
  window got small — two presentations of one list, and a width at which the app
  changed its mind. There is one now, at every width: a chip in the corner
  showing the faces of whoever is here, opening over the conversation when you
  want their names.

- **Settings live in your profile card.** They used to be a gear at the foot of
  the server rail, which is gone. The card at the foot of the column is now the
  one thing on screen that is about you rather than about a place, and it
  carries the three things that are: your status, your profile, and the app's
  settings — each named in words instead of left to a glyph.

- **Conversations read like conversations.** Messages sit in bubbles, yours on
  the right, and a run of messages from one person within a few minutes is drawn
  as one turn with the name said once at the top of it. Where the date changes
  there is a line across the column saying which day you have reached — before,
  a channel read over a week was an unbroken run of clock times with no answer to
  "was that this morning or last Thursday". The column is held to a readable
  measure and centred, so a wide window no longer runs a sentence the full width
  of the screen.

- **Two lists, one column, a tab each.** The servers and the people you know
  were stacked — servers, then a heading, then the people — which made the
  column as long as both and put whichever you wanted second below the fold of
  whichever you wanted first. They are two tabs now, each taking the whole
  column, and each carrying the count of what is unread on the other one.

  The tab is the same choice as what is beside it: picking Friends is the same
  act as opening a conversation, and opening a channel puts the tab back on
  Servers. In the shape that gives friends a window of their own there is no
  tab bar, because there is nothing to flip between.

- **Square corners.** Every corner in the app is three pixels rather than the
  eight to twenty-two it was: enough to take the bite off a corner, not enough
  to turn a column of cards into a column of lozenges. It is one token now, so
  it is one line to change. Avatars are still round, and so are the switches
  and progress bars that have to be.

- **A picture of your own behind the app, and glass in front of it.** Settings →
  Appearance takes an image from your machine and puts it behind the whole
  window, under everything. The panels then stop being solid: the navigation
  column, the pane a conversation is read on and the title bar become the same
  colours mostly transparent, softened just enough to read words over, with a
  wash between them and the picture so text survives a photograph that has its
  own bright half.

  Only the scenery. Anything you have to read *through* — a dialog, a menu, the
  box you type in, the settings screen — stays solid, which is not a matter of
  taste: a see-through settings screen with the conversation legible underneath
  it is unusable.

  The picture is copied into Ruze's own folder rather than remembered by path —
  a wallpaper that vanishes because the original was on a memory card, or in a
  folder somebody tidied, is a wallpaper that stops working for reasons nobody
  can see. It is local to the device and to the main window: nothing about it
  is published, synced or shown to anyone else, and the friends list and a
  popped-out conversation stay solid, being small windows meant to sit beside
  other things rather than backgrounds in their own right.

- **A choice of background, and the accent is green.** Light and dark decide
  how much light is in the window; a new setting beside them decides what
  colour the grey is. **Neutral** is white and a black that is actually black
  — what the app has always worn, and what it still opens in. **Warm** is paper
  and ink, the palette the rooms layout was drawn in, for anybody who would
  rather not look at pure black all day.

  The accent has moved from indigo to a sage green, which is the one colour
  that does not change between the four combinations — nor do the red, the
  presence dot or the apricot on an unread count, because those are signals and
  a signal that changes hue with a background preference is a second thing to
  learn. Every other accent the app offers is still there, indigo included.

- **The two layouts are two different apps now.** Ruze has always had a layout
  setting with two answers, and they differed only in whether a second window
  existed — the main window drew exactly the same thing either way, so the
  people you know appeared in both places at once and clicking one of them in
  the main window raised a list instead of opening a conversation.

  **One window** is everything in one column: servers, their channels and the
  people, one under the other, and everything opens where you already are.

  **A window each** is the arrangement an instant messenger has: a tall friends
  list in a window of its own, a window for every conversation you open from
  it, and a main window that is only the servers. The people are gone from its
  column — replaced by a single row saying where they went, which raises that
  window when the list is buried or closed.

- **The box you type in names the room.** "Say something in general", rather than
  "Message…". The name of the place is at the top of the page and the box is at
  the foot of it, and this is what ties the two ends together now the column is
  centred.

- **The window opens at a usable size, and stays the size you make it.** It was
  built at 800×600 every launch, which is narrower than the app wants and
  nothing to do with what you had it at last time. It opens at 1100×720 now,
  and after that at whatever size and place you left it — except maximized,
  which is the screen rather than a size somebody chose.

### Fixed

- **The ring sounds like a telephone.** It was four soft blips, because every
  sound in the app shared one envelope and that envelope is a chime's: a slow
  swell and a long fade, which is right for a bell and turns a 100 ms pulse
  into a very small one. A ring is gated instead — on fast, level, off fast —
  and it is now a hard electronic trill, two pitches swapped twenty-two times
  a second, in two bursts with a pause between them. The pause is as much of a
  telephone as the tone is.

  It repeats ten times and then stops. A phone that rings for ever is not more
  insistent, only harder to be in a room with, and the call does not end when
  the noise does — it is still there to answer.

- **A conversation's preview says when the last word was yours.** The line
  under a friend's name was the bare text of the last message, whoever sent
  it — so a message reading "you" looked like a label on the row rather than
  something somebody said. Yours are prefixed "You:" now. Theirs need nothing:
  their name is the line directly above it.

- **Calling a friend rings them, wherever they are, and rings you back.**
  Pressing call put you straight into the room, looking at your own camera,
  with nothing on screen or in the air saying whether the other person had
  been reached — and on their side, nothing rang at all unless they happened
  to be looking at your conversation at that moment. Which is very nearly the
  definition of a call nobody needed.

  Both halves are fixed. The person being called now gets the ring wherever
  they are in the app — in a channel, in settings, on somebody else's
  conversation — with their name on it and Answer and Dismiss; answering opens
  the conversation the call is in. And the caller waits on a "Calling…" screen
  with a cancel button until it is picked up, rather than being dropped into an
  empty room.

  Both ends hear the ring, which is the point of one: the person being called
  needs to know somebody wants them, and the person calling needs to know it is
  going through — silence sounds the same whether a phone is ringing or broken.
  It stops the moment the call is answered, dismissed, or given up on.

  Nothing changed underneath. A call is still a live channel on a topic both
  people work out for themselves, still with no invite message and no answer
  message to end up half-open on one side, and hanging up is still just
  leaving. What was missing was never the protocol — the backend had been
  listening on every friend's call topic all along — but anything on screen
  that watched more than one conversation at a time.

- **A conversation opens at its newest message and stays there.** Opening a
  channel scrolled to the end and then let go, which is the same thing only if
  nothing changes height afterwards — and plenty does. A picture has no size
  until it decodes, a link preview replaces its card with a player as you
  reach it, and the app's own typeface re-measures every line when it arrives.
  Each of those made the room taller after the scroll had already happened,
  and left you looking at the middle of a conversation you had asked to see
  the end of.

  It now stays at the live end while the column settles, in channels and in
  conversations both, and stops the moment you scroll up — history you are
  reading is never yanked back down by a picture loading somewhere below it.

- **A tooltip on a control near the top of the window is visible.** Ruze draws
  its own title bar, over the top of everything; the bubbles were asking
  whether there was room above them by measuring to the top of the *window*,
  so for anything in the first few rows the answer was yes and the label went
  up behind the bar, where it stayed until it timed out. They measure to the
  bottom of the bar now, and drop below the control when that is where the
  room is.

- **A friend's messages no longer arrive wearing your name.** Everything a
  friend said could be drawn as though you had said it — your username, your
  picture, on your side of the conversation — in direct messages and in every
  channel you share with them. Restarting did not help, because the mistake
  had been written down.

  Ruze decides whether a message is yours by asking whether the device that
  signed it is one of your own. That list was being added to from the wrong
  place: your card — the small document that publishes your name and picture —
  is read by your friends, and every friend is handed the key to read it when
  the friendship is made. Reading a document means joining the group that
  syncs it, so a friend appears there in exactly the way your own phone does,
  and the arrival was being taken as proof of a device rather than of a
  reader. What proves a device is being able to *write* that card, which only
  your own can, and that is the question now.

  Devices already recorded in error are taken back off. Your friends' cards
  name their own devices, and nothing they name can be one of yours, so the
  correction runs against each friend's card as Ruze starts and again whenever
  one syncs — the names come right where they stand, without another restart.

- **The accent you pick colours the whole window again.** Choosing a colour
  moved the filled buttons and the links and left the rest of the app sage:
  the send button, the channel you are reading, the badge on it, a room with
  somebody talking in it, and your own messages down the middle of a
  conversation. Every one of those is the accent at some other strength, and
  when the window became one column those tokens were the ones it was drawn
  in — but only the base colour was ever written when the setting changed, so
  eleven of the twelve swatches produced a window in two colours.

  All six now come off whatever you picked. The strengths are the sage
  defaults measured and reproduced, so choosing Sage and choosing nothing look
  the same, and the fill and the ink on it clear 6:1 for every colour in the
  row rather than only for the green they were picked against.

- **Coming back to your machine takes you off Away.** The idle timer watches
  for input that arrives at Ruze, which is the right question for going away —
  a chat window nobody has touched for half an hour is fairly described as
  unattended. It was also being used for coming back, which is a different
  question: somebody at their desk answering mail, with Ruze behind the
  browser, is not away, and Ruze had no way to know it until they happened to
  click on it. It now asks the desktop how long since anybody touched the
  machine, and treats that as being back.

  On Windows. X11 needs the screensaver extension, Wayland deliberately does
  not tell applications, and a phone has no such idea — so elsewhere the
  window's own events are still the only signal, as before.

- **Away could stick after a restart.** The window kept its own note of
  whether it had reported being idle, and that note starts empty every launch
  — while the backend's does not. So an app reopened while Away treated every
  click as "already awake" and never said otherwise. It reports once on the
  first sign of life now, which cannot disturb an Away somebody chose on
  purpose: the status you pick and the one the timer sets are kept apart.

- **Settings can be opened before you have joined anything.** The screen that
  offers to create or join a server showed your name with no way to reach
  settings from it — which is the one screen where somebody might most need
  them, since restoring an account from a backup is a thing you do *before* you
  have somewhere to be. The gear is on that screen now.

- **The friends window drew servers as initials instead of their pictures.**
  Every window is its own webview with its own copy of the app's state, so the
  main window having fetched a server's icon does nothing for the one beside
  it — and that window never asked for them. The same two servers had pictures
  in one window and coloured squares with letters on them in the other.

- **The "Leave and start" button in the live-chat prompt had invisible text.**
  It drew its label in the accent colour on a fill of the same accent colour. It
  had been that way since the prompt was added and only escaped notice because
  the accent was a mid blue that white happened to sit on too.
